references.text: The prodigal son also wished to fill himself with what was thrown to others. [ref:Luk 15:16|Luke 15:16] uses similar language about wanting to be filled (χορτασθῆναι) with what fell to others – the pigs' food – as a parallel to Lazarus's longing for the crumbs from the rich man's table.

The Canaanite woman in [ref:Matt 15:27|Matthew 15:27] says that even dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their master's table – a close parallel image to Lazarus wanting to fill himself with what falls from the rich man's table.

In [ref:Matt 7:28|Matthew 7:28] (correctly: [ref:Matt 15:27|Matt 15:27]) the crumbs from the table are mentioned again. But in [ref:Matt 7:6|Matthew 7:6] there is a warning against casting what is holy before dogs, which provides a contrast to the dogs licking Lazarus's sores.
In [ref:Dom 1:7|Judges 1:7], Adoni-Besek tells how seventy kings gathered crumbs under his table – an image of utter humiliation and dependence on others' leftovers, similar to Lazarus's situation.
Job was struck with painful boils all over his body ([ref:Job 2:7-8|Job 2:7-8]), an image of suffering and sickness that recalls the sores (ἕλκη) of Lazarus which the dogs licked.
The plague of boils in Egypt in [ref:2 Mos 9:9-11|Exodus 9:9-11] uses the same type of word for painful sores as in the description of Lazarus, showing physical suffering and humiliation.

The preceding verse [ref:Luk 16:20|Luke 16:20] introduces Lazarus and his sores, forming the immediate context for verse 21 where his distress is further described with hunger and the licking of dogs.

[ref:Ordsp 12:10|Proverbs 12:10] says that the righteous know the needs of their animals, but the wicked's mercy is cruel. The rich man's indifference toward Lazarus – while the dogs show more "compassion" – reflects this contrasting motif.
The psalmist in [ref:Sal 22:17|Psalm 22:17] describes how dogs surround him, an image of humiliation and suffering that resembles the dogs coming to the suffering Lazarus.
In [ref:1 Kong 21:19|1 Kings 21:19], the dogs lick Naboth's blood, a scene where dogs and human suffering are linked, having a thematic kinship with the dogs licking Lazarus's sores.

[ref:Luk 6:21|Luke 6:21] says "Blessed are you who now hunger, for you shall be filled." Lazarus's hunger and longing for food point forward to the eschatological comfort he receives in Abraham's bosom.
